analysis.one_liner: Abolishes the ATF and moves its firearms, arson, and alcohol-tobacco enforcement to the FBI and DEA.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2015 with two cosponsors, the bill never left a House Judiciary subcommittee and received no hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would shut down the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the federal agency that enforces the gun, explosives, and arson laws and tracks crime guns. It would immediately stop ATF from hiring, move its firearms, explosives, arson, violent crime, and domestic terrorism work to the FBI, and move its alcohol and tobacco smuggling work to the Drug Enforcement Administration. Its existing employees, cases, licenses, and property would transfer to the Justice Department, with workers protected from pay cuts for one year.
analysis.who_benefits: Gun dealers and gun-rights advocates who have long viewed ATF as an adversarial regulator, plus the FBI and DEA, which would absorb ATF's enforcement duties. Supporters also argued taxpayers would benefit from eliminating a bureau they saw as duplicative.

how_it_helps.text: Abolishes ATF outright and rescinds its hiring authority immediately, folding its firearms, explosives, arson, violent crime, and domestic terrorism enforcement into the FBI and its alcohol and tobacco smuggling enforcement into the DEA [S2][S3].
Requires a joint ATF-FBI-DEA wind-down plan that would, 'to the maximum extent practicable, without compromising core functions,' eliminate and reduce duplicative functions or waste [S3].
Protects transferred ATF personnel from separation or reduction in grade or pay for one year after the transfer [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Communities and police departments that rely on ATF's dedicated gun-trafficking investigations, arson and explosives work, and crime-gun tracing, which would move to the FBI — an agency with a much broader mission — with no guarantee of dedicated funding or staffing. ATF employees would face the disruption of an agency shutdown.

drawbacks.text: The bill would dissolve the only federal bureau dedicated to firearms, explosives, and arson enforcement, moving that work to the FBI and DEA, whose primary missions lie elsewhere, without a dedicated funding or staffing guarantee for the transferred duties [S2][S3].

Its conforming amendments would carry forward, under the FBI's name, long-standing appropriations riders that restrict the release of firearms trace data, preserving limits on public access to crime-gun tracing records [S3].
Roughly 5,000 ATF employees would be absorbed into other agencies, and the bill leaves the wind-up of pending licenses, cases, and proceedings to transition machinery that has never been tested [S3].

An honest supporter would concede the bill never identified actual savings: it required a plan to reduce 'duplicative, unnecessary functions or waste' but set no dollar figure and guaranteed the same laws would be enforced afterward by other agencies [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The claimed benefit is trimming an agency some consider duplicative, but the bill keeps every transferred law in force and simply reassigns it to the FBI and DEA, which have very different core missions. The most concrete effect for a concentrated interest is that gun dealers would no longer face a standalone bureau devoted to licensing and inspecting them and tracing crime guns, while the riders restricting public release of trace data would continue under a new name. The efficiencies were asserted, not demonstrated.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its Crime subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Representative F. James Sensenbrenner (R-WI) introduced the ATF Elimination Act on March 4, 2015; it was referred the same day to the House Judiciary Committee [S1][S5].
On March 31, 2015, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations [S5].
No further action was ever taken on the bill; it received no subcommittee hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 114th Congress ended [S5].
Only two House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: ATF itself and its workforce: the agency, its dedicated firearms and arson enforcement mission, and its crime-gun tracing operation all continued unchanged, because the bill never even reached a hearing. Nothing had to be decided, so the existing enforcement structure simply persisted.

against.name: Rep. Bob Goodlatte
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee action; after subcommittee referral in March 2015, no hearing or markup ever occurred.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was all Republican (one sponsor and two Republican cosponsors), but no vote ever occurred, so the partisan divide was never tested.

industries.note: ATF licenses and inspects gun dealers and traces crime guns; abolishing the bureau and folding enforcement into the FBI, whose mission is far broader, would end a dedicated regulator's day-to-day scrutiny of dealers. The bill also preserves, under the FBI's name, appropriations riders restricting public release of firearms trace data [S2][S3].
Would absorb ATF's firearms, explosives, arson, violent crime, and domestic terrorism enforcement along with its personnel, property, and records [S2][S3].
Would absorb ATF's alcohol and tobacco smuggling enforcement functions and related cases and personnel [S2][S3].
The bureau would be abolished, ending roughly 5,000 employees' agency, though personnel would transfer to the Justice Department with one-year protection from separation or pay cuts [S3].
